-description: Decompose batches of RHAISTRAT strategies into implementation epic DAGs. Accepts explicit IDs or a JQL query. Non-interactive.

+description: Decompose batches of RHAISTRAT strategies into implementation epic DAGs. Accepts explicit IDs or a JQL query. Use when decomposing RHAISTRAT strategy IDs into epic tasks, non-interactively.
- Priority inheritance: prerequisite epic inherits the highest priority of all HLRs it transitively enables
- An epic blocking all P0 work is implicitly P0

-- Priority split: when an epic maps to HLRs at multiple priority levels, check whether the lower-priority HLRs represent distinct, deferrable features. A feature is "distinct and deferrable" only when it could ship as its own epic with independent user value AND does not share data structures, UI surfaces, or API endpoints with the P0 work. If yes, split them into separate epics by priority so each can be planned independently. If the lower-priority HLR is incidental to the P0 work (error handling, doc coverage, config override that falls out of the same implementation) or is tightly coupled to the same implementation surface, keep it bundled — splitting tightly coupled work creates duplication and artificial boundaries.

+- Priority split: when an epic maps to HLRs at multiple priority levels, check whether the lower-priority HLRs represent distinct, deferrable features. A feature is "distinct and deferrable" only when it could ship as its own epic with independent user value AND does not share data structures, UI surfaces, or API endpoints with the P0 work. If yes, split them into separate epics by priority so each can be planned independently. If the lower-priority HLR is incidental to the P0 work (error handling, doc coverage, config override that falls out of the same implementation) or is tightly coupled to the same implementation surface, keep it bundled — splitting tightly coupled work creates duplication and artificial boundaries. **Recording contract for kept bundling:** when a lower-priority HLR is kept bundled into a higher-priority epic, the decision must be readable from the HLR Traceability Matrix row itself — mark the row `(bundled)` and state the inline rationale (why it is not separately schedulable), e.g. `| HLR-7 (P1) | E001 (bundled) — same log.Error call sites as HLR-1; a split audits the same files twice |`. A self-contained note in the summary (rationale plus the row it applies to) is also acceptable. A bare pointer ("bundled, see above") with the rationale living only in scattered prose is a defect: the bundling decision must be readable at the row.

- **Redundant / overlapping HLRs — consolidate, never split:** strategies merged from multiple sources sometimes state one capability twice in different words (e.g. "select two or more runs and view their parameters and metrics side by side" and "a diff view highlighting which parameters and metrics changed between two selected runs" — the diff view is a presentation mode of the same comparison surface over the same run data). When two HLRs describe the same data structure, UI surface, or API endpoint for the same component and team — one a restatement or presentation mode of the other — they are ONE capability: cover both with a single epic whose HLR Traceability lists both HLR ids, at the higher of the two priorities. Do not split them into separate epics by priority label: on a shared surface a P0/P1 pair is redundant wording, not a deferral signal, and splitting produces two epics building the same surface plus an artificial serialization edge between them — a boundary violation even when the second epic only extends the first's surface.

- `docs-authoring` priority exception: `docs-authoring` epics are exempt from priority inheritance. They do not push their priority upstream to the implementations they depend on. Instead, derive their priority from the strategy frontmatter `priority` field: Critical→P0, Major→P1, Normal/Minor/Undefined→P2. If the field is missing or empty, default to P2.
- **Architectural sub-system boundaries**: backend API vs. frontend plugin, Go service vs. React UI, etc.

- **Work-product type boundaries**: code implementation, content authoring (sample notebooks, tutorials, curated examples), and documentation are different kinds of work — they require different skills, different review criteria, and produce different PR review cycles. An epic that mixes code implementation with content authoring should be split even if the same team owns both. **Exception — incidental documentation touch-ups:** updating captions, screenshots, or references that fall out of a code change (no new content authored) is not a separate work stream — fold it into the originating epic as scope/acceptance criteria rather than a standalone `docs-authoring` epic. Only substantive content/documentation authoring (new tutorials, sample notebooks, curated examples, new or rewritten doc topics), or a strategy with `Documentation Support: Yes`, warrants a separate epic.

+   - **Shared-surface enforcement deliverables divide per surface, never by work type:** when a strategy's work includes an enforcement tool spanning the same surfaces other epics convert or build (a lint rule, CI check, static-analysis check, or validation harness over the converted code), do NOT carve it into a standalone work-type epic. Divide it per surface: each consuming epic authors and verifies the part of the enforcement deliverable covering its own surface, as scope plus a verification AC. Worked example — a strategy converts logging calls in two binaries and mandates a lint rule over the converted calls: the compliant shape is ONE epic per binary, each with "authors and verifies the lint rule covering its binary's converted call sites" in Scope/ACs — not an epic per binary PLUS a standalone "CI lint rule" epic. Exemption: when the enforcement tool IS the component's only implementation work (the strategy's deliverable is the tool itself), it is one epic — that is the deliverable, not an extraction.

These axes take precedence when deciding where to draw epic boundaries within a component. Step 4 may additionally split by priority when features are genuinely deferrable — but the initial boundary structure should come from architecture and work-product type, not from walking down the HLR list. Never split such that two epics must build the same data structure, UI surface, or API endpoint independently.
- Priority inversions (P0/P1/P2 inconsistent with technical complexity/reliability)
- Scope traps: ACs implying infrastructure that doesn't exist, contradictions between out-of-scope items and NFRs, storage beyond design intent

+When an epic's work is one logical change but its effort estimate sits above the ~2-week epic guideline and you keep it whole (splitting would duplicate an audit or fragment one mechanical change), do not just note the size. The Health Warnings entry must record, in this order: (1) the effort estimate, (2) the why-not-split rationale, and (3) a **concrete conditional re-split trigger** — the measurable condition under which the epic should be split after all. Compliant example: "E001 is ~1.5 sprints by the strategy's effort arithmetic; kept whole because the conversion is one mechanical pass over the same call sites and a split would audit them twice; re-split trigger: the conversion audit exceeds the strategy's 75% estimate, moving the epic past 2 sprints." A bare size acknowledgment ("noted for planning awareness") is a defect — the overage is unmanaged without the trigger. A genuinely heterogeneous epic bundling multiple work streams is different: that is a boundary problem — split it (see Epic Boundary Rules), do not paper over it with a trigger.

Look for epics that bundle work across multiple components or teams. **Also check for scope duplication across sibling epics:** compare the scope sections and acceptance criteria of all epics. If two or more epics independently build the same data structure, UI surface, API endpoint, or component (e.g., both create a benchmark list with status indicators, or both implement log viewing against the same endpoint), that is a major issue — it means the boundary was drawn incorrectly and the epics should be merged or re-split along a different axis. Minor incidental overlap (e.g., both epics mention the same config value) is not duplication. **A split that puts two presentation modes of ONE surface in two epics is duplication even though neither epic rebuilds the other's work** — e.g., a P0 epic building a side-by-side comparison view and a P1 epic building a diff view of the same data for the same team: the diff view is a thin increment on the first epic's surface, not an independent deliverable, and the correct shape is ONE epic whose HLR Traceability lists both HLRs. A priority-label difference (P0 vs P1) on the same surface is redundant requirement wording, not a boundary — flag the split as a major issue. **Also check for work-product type mixing:** if a single epic bundles code implementation with content authoring (sample notebooks, tutorials, curated examples), flag as a major issue — these are different kinds of work with different review criteria and should be separate epics even when owned by the same team.

- **Priority inheritance (lower-priority epic blocking P0 work)**: raise the blocking epic's priority to P0.

- **Parallel-edge violation (Rule 7/8/10 — an edge between implementation types that must run in parallel)**: remove the flagged entry from the dependent epic's `dependencies` list, and remove the matching edge and its justification row from the summary's DAG diagram and DAG Justification table. If the coupling between the two epics is real, express it as an acceptance criterion on the dependent epic (e.g. "the build pipeline green" AC, or "the signed attestations from the build pipeline are included and validated" for pipeline outputs consumed as content) — never as a `dependencies` edge.

+- **Standalone enforcement deliverable** (validator check 6): fold the enforcement work back per surface into the consuming epics' Scope/ACs, delete the standalone epic, and update the summary — see "Epic Boundary issues" below for the full procedure.

+- **Bundling rationale not on the record** (lower-priority HLR kept bundled, rationale only in scattered prose): add the `(bundled)` flag and the inline not-separately-schedulable rationale to the HLR Traceability Matrix row in the decomposition summary (and mirror it in the epic's HLR Traceability section). Do NOT restructure the epics or move the HLR.

- **Triage inconsistency** (`triage: below-threshold` or `docs-only` with `epic_count > 1`): The decomposer applied multi-epic logic after triage should have stopped the flow. Merge all epics back into a single epic `{ID}-E001.md`. Combine the scope, acceptance criteria, and HLR traceability from all existing epics into the single file. Delete the extra epic files and their AI signal files. Update the decomposition summary to reflect `epic_count: 1` and `critical_path_length: 1`.

- **Scope duplication across sibling epics**: Two or more epics independently build the same data structure, UI surface, or API endpoint. Merge the overlapping epics into one, or re-split along an architectural sub-system boundary (e.g., backend vs. frontend) instead of the current axis. Deduplicate acceptance criteria and scope. Delete any epic files that were merged away and update the decomposition summary.
- **Multi-component/team epic**: Split into separate epics per the component/team tuple rule. Assign new epic IDs continuing the sequence (e.g., if last epic is E007, new ones are E008, E009).
-- **Oversized epic**: Split by sub-deliverable into smaller epics.

+- **Standalone enforcement deliverable** (validator check 6 — a general Implementation epic titled as a lint rule / CI check / static-analysis check / validation harness sharing its component with another non-docs Implementation epic): fold the enforcement work back per surface — add the part covering each consuming epic's surface to that epic's Scope plus a verification AC, delete the standalone epic file (and its AI signal file), and update the decomposition summary's Epic List, DAG, and traceability matrix. Do NOT keep or renumber a standalone work-type epic.

+- **Oversized epic — classify the shape before acting:** (a) genuinely heterogeneous (multiple work streams bundled): split along the work-stream seams into separate epics. (b) One logical change above the ~2-week guideline: do NOT split — add (or complete) the Health Warnings entry with the effort estimate, the why-not-split rationale, and a concrete conditional re-split trigger. (c) The overage exists only because an enforcement deliverable was extracted into its own epic: apply the fold-back above — the overage disappears with the extracted epic.
